questions.stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a cough that has lasted more than 3 weeks. He also reports night sweats, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, decreased appetite, and low-grade fevers that spike in the evening. His sputum has recently become streaked with blood. He travels frequently on overseas mission trips. Examination shows mild lymphadenopathy and crackles over the upper lung fields. Chest radiography shows upper lobe infiltrates with slight cavitation and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Acid-fast staining of sputum shows pink, slightly bent, beaded rods. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mycobacterium intracellulare

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycobacterium leprae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Chronic cough with hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, upper lobe cavitary disease, and acid-fast bacilli in sputum is classic active tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis causes the vast majority of human mycobacterial infections and produces a slow, progressive illness with dyspnea, cough, and hemoptysis. Reactivation disease characteristically involves the upper lobes with cavitation and drains to hilar and mediastinal nodes. The organism appears as a slightly bent, beaded, acid-fast rod on Ziehl-Neelsen stain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M. avium is a Mycobacterium avium complex organism that causes severe disease almost exclusively in immunosuppressed patients, most often as lymphadenitis or disseminated infection rather than cavitary lung disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M. intracellulare is the other member of the Mycobacterium avium complex and, like M. avium, is rarely pathogenic in a person with a healthy immune system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. leprae is the mycobacterium that causes leprosy, not a chronic cavitary pulmonary infection with hemoptysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is not acid-fast and causes acute lobar pneumonia over days, not a multi-week wasting illness with cavitation.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Sputum from a 45-year-old woman with a 6-week productive cough is examined in the laboratory. A Gram stain of an adequate specimen shows no organisms. The laboratory notes that the suspected pathogen has a cell wall with a very high lipid content. Which of the following stains is most likely to demonstrate this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Giemsa stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: India ink preparation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylene blue stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silver stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain

explanation.summary: Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli demonstrated with the Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain, not with Gram stain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lipids and glycolipids of the mycobacterial cell wall prevent uptake of Gram stain, so microscopic visualization of sputum or other fluids requires a special stain. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain, also called the acid-fast stain, is used for this purpose. Mycobacteria stain pink and are therefore called acid-fast bacilli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Giemsa stain is not the special stain required to visualize the high-mycolic-acid cell wall of mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: India ink preparations demonstrate a polysaccharide capsule by negative staining and would not reveal a lipid-rich bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylene blue is used as a counterstain and for gram-negative organisms such as Neisseria; it will not highlight mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silver staining is used for organisms such as Pseudomonas and Helicobacter pylori, not for demonstrating acid-fast bacilli.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A microbiology resident notes that a bacillus recovered from a patient with chronic pneumonia cannot be visualized with Gram stain despite repeated attempts. Which of the following cell wall features best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high content of hydrophobic long-chain mycolic acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps crystal violet

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thick polysaccharide capsule external to the cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide endotoxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete absence of a cell wall in this organism

explanation.summary: Mycolic acids in the mycobacterial cell wall prevent uptake of Gram stain, which is why these organisms require acid-fast staining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacteria are protected by a lipid-containing cell wall rich in mycolic acids, in contrast to typical bacteria whose cell walls have a high peptidoglycan content. These acids cannot take up Gram stain. This is the structural reason mycobacteria are identified as acid-fast bacilli rather than as gram-positive or gram-negative organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A thick peptidoglycan layer is the feature of gram-positive organisms, which retain crystal violet and stain readily; mycobacteria have relatively little peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A polysaccharide capsule does not block Gram staining of the underlying cell; encapsulated organisms are still visible on Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lipopolysaccharide-rich outer membrane is a gram-negative feature; such organisms still take up Gram stain and appear pink.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycobacteria do have a cell wall; it is its lipid composition, not its absence, that defeats Gram staining.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A physician suspects pulmonary tuberculosis and submits a sputum specimen for culture, making a special request of the laboratory. Growth of this organism requires a particular medium on which it forms large colonies with a waxy appearance. Which of the following media is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chocolate agar

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lowenstein-Jensen medium

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacConkey agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sheep blood agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thayer-Martin selective medium

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis requires special media, most commonly Lowenstein-Jensen medium, on which it forms large waxy colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacteria will not grow on routine culture media, so a specific laboratory request must be made when tuberculosis is suspected. Lowenstein-Jensen medium is the common medium used. Because the organism grows slowly, detection can take up to 10 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chocolate agar is a routine enriched medium used for fastidious organisms such as Neisseria and Haemophilus, not for mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MacConkey agar is selective for gram-negative enteric bacilli and does not support growth of mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blood agar is a general-purpose medium used for organisms such as Pseudomonas and streptococci; mycobacteria will not grow on it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thayer-Martin agar is a selective medium for pathogenic Neisseria species and has no role in mycobacterial culture.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A sputum smear from an immunosuppressed patient shows pink bacilli on acid-fast stain. The laboratory reports that this result alone cannot establish which mycobacterial species is present and recommends culture or polymerase chain reaction testing. Which of the following best explains this limitation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria also stain acid-fast and look identical

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal respiratory flora in sputum also retain the acid-fast dye strongly

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stain binds host inflammatory cells rather than bacterial cell walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stain cannot distinguish living organisms from organisms already killed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The stain detects organisms only when they are present in very large numbers

explanation.summary: Acid-fast staining is nonspecific among mycobacteria, so culture or PCR is needed to identify the species.
explanation.whyCorrect: The acid-fast stain will show pink bacilli whenever a mycobacterium is present, but some non-tuberculosis mycobacteria stain acid-fast as well. There is no reliable way to differentiate M. tuberculosis from other mycobacteria microscopically. In uncertain cases, a culture or PCR analysis is required for organism identification.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ordinary respiratory flora are not acid-fast, so they are not the source of the ambiguity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stain highlights the mycolic-acid-rich bacterial cell wall, which is exactly why mycobacteria appear pink.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Viability is not what is in question here; even a smear full of viable bacilli would not reveal the species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sensitivity at low organism burden is not the stated problem; the issue is that a positive smear does not identify which mycobacterium is present.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A public health officer investigates two clusters of mycobacterial lung disease. In the first cluster, caused by M. tuberculosis, every case could be traced to contact with another infected person. In the second cluster, caused by Mycobacterium avium complex, no person-to-person link could be established. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: M. tuberculosis is acquired by the fecal-oral route, while Mycobacterium avium complex is inhaled

choices.label: B
choices.text: M. tuberculosis lives only in the human respiratory tract, while MAC lives in the environment

choices.label: C
choices.text: M. tuberculosis survives in soil and water, while Mycobacterium avium complex is carried only by humans

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are not acid-fast and therefore cannot spread between people

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex requires an arthropod vector, while M. tuberculosis spreads in droplets

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis has no environmental reservoir and spreads person to person, whereas Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are environmental.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis is not found in the environment; its only reservoir is the human respiratory tract, where it lies dormant and is later spread by coughing if disease reactivates. Mycobacterium avium complex bacilli are common environmental organisms found in soil, water, and animals. Patients acquire them by inhaling bacilli from those sources rather than from another person.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M. tuberculosis is contracted by respiratory inhalation, not orally, so the fecal-oral route does not apply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two organisms: M. tuberculosis is the one restricted to humans, and Mycobacterium avium complex is the environmental group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacterium avium complex organisms are acid-fast; indeed, that is why an acid-fast smear cannot distinguish them from M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither organism requires an arthropod vector; Mycobacterium avium complex is acquired from contaminated soil, water, or animals.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A research laboratory grows a clinical isolate of M. tuberculosis and observes that the bacilli aggregate into long, serpentine ropelike bundles. The responsible cell wall component is also toxic to mammalian cells and inhibits neutrophil migration. Which of the following is this component?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cord factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipoarabinomannan

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipopolysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptidoglycan

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purified protein derivative

explanation.summary: Cord factor is toxic to mammalian cells, inhibits neutrophil migration, and produces the characteristic long serpentine colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cord factor is one of the proposed virulence factors of M. tuberculosis. It damages mammalian cells directly and blocks neutrophils from migrating to the site of infection. It also causes the bacilli to grow in the long, cord-like serpentine arrangements from which it takes its name.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokine release and helps the organism resist host oxidative stress; it does not produce serpentine cords.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is an outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria and is not a mycobacterial virulence factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is present in small amounts in mycobacteria and is not responsible for cord formation or neutrophil inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Purified protein derivative is the antigen preparation injected for the tuberculin skin test, not a virulence factor.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Alveolar macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis generate reactive oxygen species in an attempt to kill the organism. One mycobacterial cell wall component both induces host cytokine production and allows the organism to withstand this oxidative stress. Which of the following is this component?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cord factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipoarabinomannan

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycolic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nitric oxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teichoic acid

explanation.summary: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokines and enables M. tuberculosis to resist host oxidative stress.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipoarabinomannan is listed among the proposed virulence factors of M. tuberculosis. It stimulates the release of host cytokines and confers resistance to the oxidative killing mechanisms of the macrophage. This contributes to the organism's ability to persist inside the phagocyte that ingested it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cord factor is toxic to mammalian cells and inhibits neutrophil migration; resistance to oxidative stress is not its described role.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycolic acid confers natural antibiotic resistance and immune evasion through extreme hydrophobicity rather than by defeating oxidative stress.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is an antibacterial compound produced by the activated macrophage to kill the bacilli, not a mycobacterial product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teichoic acid is a gram-positive cell wall constituent and is not part of the mycobacterial cell wall.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: An isolate of M. tuberculosis is found to be intrinsically resistant to many traditional antibiotics and also evades the host immune response. Both properties are attributed to extremely hydrophobic long-chain fatty acids in its cell wall. Which of the following components is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capsular polysaccharide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cord factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipoarabinomannan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycolic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptidoglycan

explanation.summary: Mycolic acids are long-chain, extremely hydrophobic fatty acids that convey natural antibiotic resistance and help mycobacteria evade the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycolic acid is the defining structural feature of the mycobacterial cell wall. Its high content makes the bacillus tough and resistant to damage, conveys natural antibiotic resistance, and helps the organism evade host immunity. It also slows growth, which is why mycobacterial infections tend to be chronic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A polysaccharide capsule is not described as a mycobacterial virulence factor in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cord factor is defined by its toxicity to mammalian cells and inhibition of neutrophil migration, not by conveying broad antibiotic resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipoarabinomannan induces cytokines and resists oxidative stress; it is not the component that confers natural antibiotic resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptidoglycan is the major wall constituent of typical bacteria, and mycobacteria are distinguished by having relatively little of it.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: After inhalation, M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages but continues to replicate inside them. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this intracellular survival?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism escapes from the phagosome and replicates freely in the cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism lyses the macrophage within minutes of being ingested by it

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism replicates only outside cells, within the alveolar lining fluid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism secretes a capsule that prevents opsonization by complement proteins

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bacillus lives within phagosomes of alveolar macrophages. Normally phagosomes fuse with lysosomes, which supply the enzymes needed to kill the organism. M. tuberculosis prevents this fusion by blocking macrophage intracellular calcium and acidification, so the bacilli grow within the phagocyte rather than being destroyed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The organism remains within phagosomes rather than escaping into the cytoplasm; that is where its growth occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rapid lysis of the macrophage is not the mechanism of early survival; the bacilli first grow quietly within intact macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary infection is characterized by macrophage invasion and intracellular growth, not extracellular replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The bacterial surface is in fact coated with C3b, which promotes rather than prevents recognition by complement receptors.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient's M. tuberculosis isolate is reported by the laboratory as multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Resistance to which of the following is required for this designation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fluoroquinolone and another second-line drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isoniazid and a fluoroquinolone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isoniazid and a second-line injectable agent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isoniazid and rifampicin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rifampicin and a fluoroquinolone

explanation.summary: MDR-TB is defined by resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotic resistance is one of the virulence properties of M. tuberculosis. When an isolate is resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin, the disease is referred to as multidrug-resistant TB. Such resistance limits treatment options, extends treatment time, and increases cost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance to a fluoroquinolone plus another second-line drug is what is added on top of MDR-TB to make an isolate extensively drug-resistant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoroquinolone resistance belongs to the definition of extensively drug-resistant TB, not to the definition of MDR-TB.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Resistance to a second-line injectable agent is part of extensively drug-resistant disease rather than the MDR-TB definition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance to a fluoroquinolone is a feature of extensively drug-resistant disease, and rifampicin resistance alone does not define MDR-TB.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: An isolate of M. tuberculosis that is already resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin is additionally found to be resistant to a fluoroquinolone and to at least one other second-line drug. How is this isolate best classified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atypical (non-tuberculous) mycobacterial infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fully drug-susceptible tuberculosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Latent tuberculosis infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis

explanation.summary: Extensively drug-resistant TB is MDR-TB that is additionally resistant to a fluoroquinolone and at least one other second-line agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDR-TB denotes resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone and at least one further second-line drug. Each step up in resistance further limits treatment options, lengthens therapy, and raises the cost of care substantially.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atypical mycobacteria refers to the Mycobacterium avium complex organisms, not to a resistant M. tuberculosis isolate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The isolate is resistant to at least four agents, so it is by definition not drug-susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent infection describes an asymptomatic walled-off infection, a clinical state, not a drug-resistance pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multidrug-resistant disease stops at resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin; this isolate has additional second-line resistance.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 24-year-old nursing student with a documented negative tuberculin skin test is exposed to a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Eight weeks later she feels well and her chest radiograph is normal, but her tuberculin skin test is now positive. Which of the following events in the natural history of tuberculosis has most likely occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct bacterial infection of the skin at the injection site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Miliary dissemination of bacilli through the bloodstream

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary infection with growth inside alveolar macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive primary tuberculosis with tissue destruction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of a long-standing latent infection

explanation.summary: Conversion of the tuberculin skin test after exposure marks primary infection, in which bacilli invade and grow within alveolar macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary (initial) infection begins after airborne exposure, with macrophage invasion and intracellular growth within macrophages. It is during this phase that the tuberculin skin test turns positive. The patient can be entirely asymptomatic, because cellular immunity usually contains the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A positive tuberculin reaction is an immune response to injected protein antigen, not an infection of the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Miliary disease produces an acutely ill patient with tiny disseminated lesions, not an asymptomatic person with a normal radiograph.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive primary tuberculosis means the immune system cannot suppress the infection and the patient develops symptoms, which she has not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivation occurs months to years after a latent infection is already established, and her skin test was negative only 8 weeks ago.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Among people newly infected with M. tuberculosis, the granuloma often isolates the bacilli and halts spread before appreciable lung damage occurs. Approximately what proportion of infected patients develop this latent form of infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 5 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 25 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 90 percent

explanation.summary: Latent infection, the most common outcome of primary tuberculosis, occurs in about 90 percent of infected patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: In latent infection the granuloma effectively isolates the growing bacilli from surrounding tissue and stops the spread of infection before appreciable lung damage occurs. More than 90 percent of patients remain asymptomatic for years, and some recover completely. Most patients with tuberculosis are therefore diagnosed during latency by a screening test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 5 percent is the proportion of latently infected patients who later reactivate, not the proportion who become latent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 10 percent is the fraction that instead progresses to progressive primary disease, not the fraction becoming latent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A quarter underestimates the proportion contained by the granuloma and would imply most patients progress.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Half is far too low; latent infection is described as by far the most common outcome of primary infection.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a positive screening test for tuberculosis, a normal chest radiograph, and no symptoms. His family asks whether he can transmit the infection to them at home. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is infectious because all infected people shed bacilli constantly

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is infectious only at times when he is coughing

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is infectious through contaminated food and drinking water

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is infectious until his screening test becomes negative

choices.label: E
choices.text: He is not infectious, because only active disease is transmissible

explanation.summary: Patients with latent tuberculosis are not infectious; only patients with active disease transmit the organism.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a patient has active tuberculosis they are extremely infectious, because bacilli are discharged into exhaled air. Patients with latent tuberculosis are not infectious, since the bacilli remain walled off inside granulomas. An asymptomatic patient with a positive screening test and a normal chest radiograph has latent infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most infected patients are latently infected and shed no bacilli at all; only active disease produces infectious aerosols.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coughing spreads bacilli only when active disease has released organisms into the airways, which has not happened here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. tuberculosis is contracted by respiratory inhalation, not by the oral route, so food and water are not vehicles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening tests can stay positive for years after infection is cleared, so they are not a measure of infectiousness.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant with untreated HIV infection develops a chronic cough, low-grade fever, and failure to thrive several weeks after household exposure to a relative with active tuberculosis. Which of the following clinical phases of tuberculosis best describes this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cleared infection with residual memory T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Healed Ghon complex with fibrosis and calcification

choices.label: C
choices.text: Latent infection with walled-off bacilli

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive primary tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis

explanation.summary: When the immune system cannot suppress the initial infection and symptoms follow directly, the patient has progressive primary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In progressive primary tuberculosis the immune system cannot contain the initial infection and the at-risk patient develops symptoms, usually small children and immunosuppressed patients such as those with AIDS. Bacilli replicate within macrophages until rupture, releasing organisms that infect adjacent macrophages. Mild dry cough, low-grade fever, fatigue, weight loss, and failure to thrive in infants are typical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cleared infection leaves a well child with only immunologic memory, which does not fit this ill infant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A healed Ghon complex represents containment by fibrosis and calcification and would not produce failure to thrive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Latent infection is asymptomatic by definition; this infant is symptomatic within weeks of exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivation occurs months to years after latency is established, not in the weeks immediately following a first exposure.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A woman with documented latent tuberculosis asks about her chance of later developing active disease. Approximately what percentage of patients with latent infection go on to reactivate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 20 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 90 percent

explanation.summary: About 5 percent of patients with latent tuberculosis reactivate into secondary, active disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In latent infection the bacilli lie dormant within a granuloma with minimal growth for months or years. In roughly 5 percent of cases the infection reactivates, usually two or more years later. This phase is called secondary or reactivation tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One percent understates the reactivation risk that makes latent infection worth screening for and treating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Twenty percent is well above the reactivation rate described for latent tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Half of latently infected patients do not reactivate; the great majority remain asymptomatic for years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 90 percent is the proportion of infected patients who become latent, not the proportion who reactivate.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with known latent tuberculosis is about to begin therapy for a newly diagnosed autoimmune disease. Which of the following features of his history most increases his risk of reactivation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A remote history of pneumococcal pneumonia in childhood

choices.label: B
choices.text: A strong family history of asthma and atopy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequent long-distance air travel for his work

choices.label: D
choices.text: Planned long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receipt of an influenza vaccine earlier this month

explanation.summary: Immune suppression, such as corticosteroid therapy, is a well-recognized precipitant of reactivation of latent tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Known precipitants of reactivation include immune suppression from corticosteroid drugs or HIV/AIDS, which reduces the number or functionality of Th1 cells, as well as chronic illnesses such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and lymphoma, and tobacco smoking. Because multiple immunosuppressants used to treat autoimmune disease increase this risk, tuberculosis screening is suggested before these treatments are started.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A past bacterial pneumonia does not impair Th1-mediated containment of dormant bacilli and is not a listed precipitant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A family history of atopy does not suppress cell-mediated immunity and is not among the recognized triggers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Travel may affect exposure risk but does not cause an already established latent infection to reactivate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Influenza vaccination does not produce immune suppression and is not associated with reactivation.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with diabetes who had a positive tuberculin skin test 20 years ago now has a productive cough, fever, night sweats, and hemoptysis. Which of the following chest radiographic findings is most characteristic of his current disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A completely normal chest radiograph despite his symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: A peripheral subpleural lower lobe nodule with enlarged hilar nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilateral pleural effusions without any parenchymal abnormality

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cavitation and consolidation involving the upper lobes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dense lobar consolidation limited to the right middle lobe

explanation.summary: Reactivation tuberculosis characteristically produces upper lobe cavities and consolidation.
explanation.whyCorrect: During reactivation, enlarging granulomas undergo central necrosis, producing cavities and upper lobe consolidations visible on chest imaging. Reactivation typically starts in the upper lobes of the lungs. Granulomas may then break into a bronchus, and endothelial damage causes the hemoptysis seen in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal radiograph fits latent infection, but this man has symptoms of active cavitary disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A peripheral subpleural nodule with hilar adenopathy describes the Ghon complex of primary infection, not reactivation disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated pleural effusions without parenchymal disease are not the characteristic pattern of reactivation tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dense lobar consolidation of a single lower or middle lobe is the pattern of typical bacterial pneumonia.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient with reactivation tuberculosis is admitted to a negative-pressure isolation room because he is now highly infectious, although he was asymptomatic and noninfectious for many years. Which of the following events best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A necrotic granuloma has ruptured into a bronchus, releasing bacilli into the air

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacilli are released into the pleural space from a thickened pleural surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacilli are shed in the stool after seeding of the intestinal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacilli reach the skin through the bloodstream and are shed from lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacilli travel from an infected hilar lymph node directly through the chest wall

explanation.summary: Reactivation makes a patient infectious when a necrotic granuloma ruptures into a bronchus and bacilli enter exhaled air.
explanation.whyCorrect: During reactivation, enlarging granulomas undergo central necrosis. These granulomas may break into a bronchus, discharging M. tuberculosis into exhaled air and making the patient infectious. Latent patients, whose bacilli remain sealed inside intact granulomas, are not infectious.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pleural thickening accompanies the Ghon focus, and the pleural space does not communicate with exhaled air.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. tuberculosis is spread by inhaled droplets coughed into the air, not by shedding in stool.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hematogenous spread to skin and other organs causes extrapulmonary disease but is not how the organism is transmitted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hilar lymph nodes drain bacilli inward through lymphatics; they do not discharge organisms through the chest wall.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A severely immunosuppressed patient with reactivated tuberculosis becomes acutely ill. Chest radiography shows innumerable tiny, uniformly distributed nodules throughout both lungs, and additional lesions are found in the liver and spine. Which of the following best describes this pattern of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ghon complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latent tuberculosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Localized cavitary tuberculosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Miliary tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tuberculous lymphadenitis

explanation.summary: Widespread bloodborne dissemination producing tiny seed-like lesions throughout the body is miliary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some cases, especially with immune suppression, bacilli spread to other organs such as bone, skin, liver, brain, and spine, or disseminate widely through the bloodstream. This produces miliary tuberculosis, characterized by tiny, seed-like lesions throughout the body. It most commonly occurs during reactivation of latent infection but can also develop during primary infection in severely immunosuppressed patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Ghon complex is a localized peripheral focus with thickened pleura and hilar adenopathy, not diffuse seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latent tuberculosis is asymptomatic with bacilli confined to granulomas and would not produce liver and spine lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Localized cavitary disease is confined to the upper lobes and does not give a uniform diffuse nodular pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculous lymphadenitis involves node enlargement rather than innumerable parenchymal nodules in multiple organs.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Autopsy of a patient who had an asymptomatic primary tuberculosis infection shows a small, yellow-white granuloma containing few bacilli located in the lung periphery, just beneath the pleura. Which of the following terms best describes this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronchiectatic cyst

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cavitary lesion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ghon complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ghon focus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Miliary nodule

explanation.summary: A Ghon focus is the yellow-white peripheral granuloma containing few bacilli that forms during primary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: During primary tuberculosis a Ghon focus, a granuloma containing few bacteria, can form. These lesions are yellow-white and are usually found in the lung periphery near the pleura. The overlying pleura may thicken in response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchiectasis is a complication described with Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease, not the primary lesion of tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cavities arise when enlarging granulomas undergo central necrosis during reactivation, typically in the upper lobes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Ghon complex also requires thickened pleura and hilar lymphadenopathy, not just the parenchymal focus alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Miliary nodules are innumerable tiny lesions produced by widespread hematogenous dissemination, not a single peripheral granuloma.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A radiologist reviewing films from a patient with healed primary tuberculosis describes a peripheral parenchymal lesion, thickening of the pleura overlying it, and enlarged hilar lymph nodes. Together, these three findings are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Ghon complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: An isolated Ghon focus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Caseating tuberculous pleuritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cavitary reactivation disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Miliary tuberculosis

explanation.summary: The Ghon complex is the Ghon focus together with thickened pleura and hilar lymphadenopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacilli from the Ghon focus drain through the lymphatics to the neighboring hilar lymph nodes, which lie on the medial surface of the lungs surrounded by the bronchi and pulmonary vessels. The entire structure containing the Ghon focus, the thickened pleura, and the hilar lymphadenopathy is the Ghon complex. It is one of the typical radiographic signs sought when evaluating a patient for tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The Ghon focus is only the parenchymal granuloma; it does not include the pleural and nodal components described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleural thickening here is part of the complex; isolated caseating pleuritis does not describe these three findings together.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cavitary disease of reactivation involves upper lobe necrosis and consolidation, not a healed peripheral complex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Miliary disease produces innumerable tiny lesions distributed throughout the lungs and other organs.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Roughly 7 to 21 days after primary infection, an immunocompetent host walls off M. tuberculosis within an organized structure that establishes an equilibrium between bacterial killing and bacterial growth. Which of the following best describes the cells that make up this structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial cells forming new capillaries around the bacilli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eosinophils and mast cells clustered around the bacilli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infected macrophages, uninfected macrophages, and recruited T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils and fibrin surrounding a liquefied purulent necrotic center

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma cells actively secreting organism-specific antibody

explanation.summary: The tuberculous granuloma is built from infected and uninfected macrophages plus recruited T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: When patients have a healthy immune system but cannot completely kill M. tuberculosis, the organism stimulates macrophages to form early granulomas. These are collections of infected macrophages, non-infected macrophages, and T cells recruited to help fight the infection. These immune cells form a barrier around the infection, and multinucleated giant cells and lymphocytes are seen at its margins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: New capillary formation is a feature of granulation tissue in wound healing, not the defining content of a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils and mast cells are features of allergic and parasitic responses, not of tuberculous granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils and fibrin around a purulent center describe an abscess; cord factor actually inhibits neutrophil migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defense against M. tuberculosis depends on cellular immunity with Th1 cells and macrophages rather than on antibody.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A lung biopsy from an immunocompetent patient with chronic cough shows well-formed granulomas, but the pathologist notes that there is no central caseous necrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this specimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conclude that the patient must be severely immunocompromised

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perform a Gram stain of the tissue to identify the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform a special stain for acid-fast organisms on the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the biopsy from a different lobe of the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Report the specimen as inconsistent with mycobacterial infection

explanation.summary: Whenever granulomas are present, a special stain for acid-fast organisms is indicated regardless of whether caseous necrosis is seen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The usual tubercle in a person with cell-mediated immunity shows central granular caseation surrounded by epithelioid and multinucleate giant cells. However, even in immunocompetent patients tubercular granulomas occasionally show no central caseation. For that reason, the presence or absence of caseous necrosis does not exclude mycobacterial infection, and acid-fast staining is indicated whenever granulomas are present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Noncaseating granulomas occur in immunocompetent patients as well, so no conclusion about immune status is warranted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mycobacteria do not take up Gram stain because of their mycolic acid content, so this would be uninformative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rebiopsy is unnecessary when a simple special stain can be applied to the tissue already obtained.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of caseation does not rule out tuberculosis, so the specimen cannot be dismissed on that basis.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Within a week of inhaling M. tuberculosis, infected alveolar macrophages secrete a cytokine that activates natural killer cells and induces naive CD4+ T cells to differentiate into Th1 cells. Which of the following is this cytokine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interferon-gamma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-12

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interleukin-6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha

explanation.summary: Interleukin-12 from infected macrophages activates NK cells and drives Th1 differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: After bacteria reach the alveoli, cellular immunity involving Th1 T helper cells and macrophages is the host's best defense. IL-12 secreted from infected macrophages activates natural killer cells and induces the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into Th1 cells. Those cells then supply the interferon that activates macrophage killing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interferon-gamma is secreted by NK cells and Th1 cells downstream of this step; it is the effector, not the inducer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-4 is not among the cytokines described in the macrophage response to M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukin-6 is described in disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease as a driver of systemic symptoms, not of Th1 differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha likewise contributes to the systemic features of MAC bacteremia rather than to NK cell activation here.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Natural killer cells and Th1 cells in a patient with early tuberculosis secrete a cytokine that activates macrophages and enhances their ability to kill intracellular mycobacteria, in part through production of nitric oxide. Which of the following is this cytokine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interferon-gamma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-10

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interleukin-6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha

explanation.summary: Interferon-gamma from NK and Th1 cells activates macrophages to kill intracellular mycobacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferon-gamma is secreted by natural killer cells and Th1 cells. This cytokine activates macrophages and enhances their ability to kill the intracellular mycobacteria within them. Antibacterial compounds such as nitric oxide, produced by the activated macrophage, then kill the bacilli.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-10 is not described among the mediators of the protective response to M. tuberculosis in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-12 comes from the infected macrophage and acts upstream, activating NK cells and driving Th1 differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukin-6 is associated with the systemic symptoms of disseminated MAC infection rather than macrophage activation here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is described in MAC bacteremia as a cause of fever and cachexia, not as the macrophage-activating signal.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient with advanced HIV infection develops active tuberculosis. In addition to loss of CD4+ T cells, which of the following immune defects described in HIV-infected patients contributes to their susceptibility to tuberculosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent immunoglobulin A at mucosal surfaces

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent neutrophil oxidative burst activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficient mast cell degranulation responses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deficient production of complement protein C3b

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deficient production of interleukin-12

explanation.summary: Many HIV-infected patients are IL-12 deficient, which is one mechanism by which AIDS patients become susceptible to tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-12 from infected macrophages is required to activate NK cells and drive naive CD4+ T cells toward the Th1 phenotype. Many patients infected with HIV are IL-12 deficient, so this arm of cellular immunity is impaired. Because Th1 cells and activated macrophages are the principal defense against M. tuberculosis, these patients are highly susceptible to tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucosal IgA is not the protective mechanism against an organism that survives inside alveolar macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophils are not the central defense against M. tuberculosis, and cord factor already inhibits their migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cell function has no described role in containment of mycobacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C3b coating of the bacterial surface is what triggers macrophage phagocytosis; a deficiency of it is not the described HIV defect.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A health care worker receives an intradermal injection of purified protein derivative, and the site is examined for inflammation 48 to 72 hours later. Which of the following immunologic reactions accounts for a positive result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A type I reaction mediated by IgE bound to mast cells in the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: A type II reaction mediated by antibody against host cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: A type III reaction mediated by immune complex deposition

choices.label: D
choices.text: A type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by memory T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Local bacterial replication within the injected skin site

explanation.summary: A positive tuberculin skin test is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction driven by memory T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: For the PPD skin test, proteins from the cell envelope of Mycobacterium species are injected subcutaneously and inflammation is checked 48 to 72 hours later. A positive reaction is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction in which memory T cells acquired from infection are recruited to the injection site, release cytokines, and cause swelling. The delay of one to three days reflects the time needed for this cellular response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes, not over 48 to 72 hours, and involve wheal and flare rather than induration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody directed against host cell surfaces does not explain a localized delayed induration to injected protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune complex deposition produces vasculitic injury and is not the mechanism of the tuberculin reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only purified protein, not live organisms, is injected, so no bacterial replication occurs at the site.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman who immigrated 3 years ago and received the BCG vaccine as an adolescent requires screening for latent tuberculosis before starting an immunosuppressive medication. She is asymptomatic and produces no sputum. Which of the following tests is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interferon-gamma release assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification test of sputum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sputum culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tuberculin skin test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain of sputum

explanation.summary: After recent BCG vaccination the interferon-gamma release assay is preferred, because BCG causes false-positive tuberculin skin tests.
explanation.whyCorrect: BCG vaccination can cause false positives on the PPD skin test, usually when the vaccine was administered within 10 years, so alternative screening should be considered in these patients. The interferon-gamma release assay does not give false positives after BCG vaccination or after non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection. It is also a reasonable choice because screening is recommended before immunosuppressive therapy is started.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nucleic acid amplification of sputum is used for rapid diagnosis of active tuberculosis, not for latent infection screening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Culture is used to confirm and characterize active infection and is very slow; it is not a latent infection screening test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The tuberculin skin test is exactly the test likely to be falsely positive because of her relatively recent BCG vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acid-fast staining of sputum is a test for active disease and is not useful in an asymptomatic patient producing no sputum.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory plans to replace the tuberculin skin test with the interferon-gamma release assay for routine latent tuberculosis screening. Which of the following is a genuine advantage of the newer assay?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes negative once a previous infection has been fully cleared

choices.label: B
choices.text: It costs less than the skin test and requires no laboratory processing

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not falsely positive after BCG vaccination or other mycobacterial infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides a result within a few minutes at the patient's bedside, without a laboratory

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reliably distinguishes latent infection from active tuberculosis disease

explanation.summary: The interferon-gamma release assay avoids the false positives that BCG vaccination and non-tuberculous mycobacteria cause with the skin test.
explanation.whyCorrect: In this assay the patient's blood is mixed with antigens derived from and specific to M. tuberculosis, and T cells specific for those antigens release interferon-gamma. Because the antigens are specific to M. tuberculosis, the assay does not produce false positives in people who have had the BCG vaccine or a non-tuberculosis mycobacterial infection. It also does not depend on the patient returning to have the arm examined.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Past infections still trigger a positive result, which is a shared limitation of both screening tests.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The assay is more expensive than the skin test and requires laboratory work, which is time consuming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The need for blood collection and laboratory processing means results are not available within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Like the skin test, it is a screening test for infection and does not by itself separate latent from active disease.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis has sputum sent for acid-fast smear, culture, and nucleic acid amplification testing. Which of the following is an additional benefit of the nucleic acid amplification test in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It distinguishes a latent infection from one that has been cleared

choices.label: B
choices.text: It identifies every drug resistance that the isolate carries within hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes the need for chest radiography in staging the disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns positive before the patient becomes able to infect others

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some panels simultaneously screen the specimen for rifampicin resistance

explanation.summary: Beyond rapid detection, some nucleic acid amplification panels also screen for rifampicin resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: A combination of sputum stain, radiology, and nucleic acid amplification testing is usually used to rapidly diagnose active tuberculosis. One additional benefit of the amplification test is that some panels also screen for rifampicin resistance, which matters because resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin defines MDR-TB. Culture, while very slow, is still needed to identify any further resistances.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The test detects organism nucleic acid in sputum and is a test for active disease, not a way to classify latency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only some resistances are covered by these panels; culture is still required to identify further resistances.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-rays remain part of the workup, used to assess the extent of lung disease and look for signs such as a Ghon complex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sputum testing requires a patient who has symptoms and produces sputum, which is well after infectiousness begins.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with AIDS has several weeks of fever, night sweats, and diarrhea, and blood cultures grow an acid-fast organism identified as Mycobacterium avium. Which of the following laboratory findings would most strongly have predicted his risk for this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A CD4+ T-cell count below 100 cells per cubic millimeter

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hemoglobin concentration below 8 grams per deciliter

choices.label: C
choices.text: A platelet count below 50,000 per cubic millimeter

choices.label: D
choices.text: A serum immunoglobulin A level below the reference range

choices.label: E
choices.text: An absolute neutrophil count below 500 per cubic millimeter

explanation.summary: HIV infection with a high viral load and a CD4+ T-cell count below 100 cells per cubic millimeter is the major risk factor for MAC infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: MAC bacilli rarely cause infection in patients with healthy immune systems but often cause disease in those with immunodeficiency. The listed risk factors are HIV infection with high viral load and low CD4+ T-cell counts below 100 cells per cubic millimeter, immunosuppression from disease or immunosuppressive therapies, and deficiencies in interferon-gamma production or function. Disseminated disease in such patients may be fatal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anemia is a consequence of disseminated MAC bacteremia rather than a predictor of acquiring the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombocytopenia is not a described risk factor for Mycobacterium avium complex disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low immunoglobulin A is not among the risk factors described for Mycobacterium avium complex infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia predisposes to pyogenic and fungal infection; defense against mycobacteria depends on cell-mediated immunity.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient with advanced immunosuppression is diagnosed with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection. His family asks how he could have caught it, since no one they know has been ill. Which of the following statements about acquisition of this organism is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is acquired by inhaling bacilli from contaminated soil, water, or animals

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is acquired only from respiratory droplets coughed by an infected person

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is acquired through the bite of an infected arthropod vector

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is acquired through transfusion of contaminated blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is acquired when a latent childhood lung focus reactivates

explanation.summary: MAC organisms are environmental and are acquired from contaminated soil, water, or animals rather than from another person.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike M. tuberculosis, MAC bacilli are common environmental organisms. Patients become infected when they inhale the bacilli from contaminated soil, water, or animals, not by person-to-person transmission. The bacilli enter the body through both respiratory and gastrointestinal cells and can then cause local or disseminated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Person-to-person droplet spread is the route for M. tuberculosis, whose only reservoir is the human respiratory tract.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No arthropod vector is involved in the acquisition of Mycobacterium avium complex organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion is not a described route of acquisition; environmental exposure is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The MAC disease mechanism is very different from that of M. tuberculosis in that it does not involve latent and reactivation disease.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common local manifestation of Mycobacterium avium complex infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cavitary pneumonia of the upper lobes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infective endocarditis with valve destruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphadenitis with fever and node enlargement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meningitis with cranial nerve palsies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertebral osteomyelitis with back pain

explanation.summary: Lymphadenitis is the most common local manifestation of Mycobacterium avium complex infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once MAC enters the body it can cause local or disseminated disease. The most common local manifestation is lymphadenitis, causing fever and enlargement of lymph nodes. The nodes involved are most often cervical, mediastinal, or abdominal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Upper lobe cavitary pneumonia is the classic picture of reactivation tuberculosis rather than of MAC infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endocarditis is not among the described manifestations of Mycobacterium avium complex infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meningitis is described as a site of extrapulmonary spread in progressive primary tuberculosis, not as typical MAC disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebral involvement is a site seeded in miliary tuberculosis and is not the usual local MAC manifestation.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A patient with AIDS and Mycobacterium avium complex bacteremia has fever, night sweats, cachexia, anemia, diarrhea, and enlarged lymph nodes. Elevated serum levels of which of the following pairs of mediators best account for these systemic findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histamine and bradykinin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-10 and transforming growth factor-beta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-12 and interferon-gamma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interleukin-4 and interleukin-5

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-6

explanation.summary: MAC bacteremia raises serum tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-6, producing fever, night sweats, cachexia, anemia, and diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: In disseminated disease, MAC bacteremia can cause elevated serum levels of tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-6. These mediators produce fever, night sweats, cachexia, anemia, diarrhea from enteritis, and lymph node enlargement. In severe cases this picture can resemble miliary tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine and bradykinin mediate immediate hypersensitivity and vascular permeability, not this chronic wasting syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-10 and transforming growth factor-beta are not the mediators described as causing these systemic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-12 and interferon-gamma are the protective Th1 mediators; deficient interferon function is in fact a risk factor for MAC disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukin-4 and interleukin-5 drive allergic and eosinophilic responses and are not implicated in MAC bacteremia.

questions.topicName: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium Avium Complex

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with 4 days of fever to 104.5 F, nonproductive cough, headache, and watery diarrhea. He stayed at a hotel one week ago, and two other guests from the same hotel have been admitted with pneumonia. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L. Chest radiograph shows a dense lower lobe consolidation, and a urine antigen test is positive. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Hotel or cooling-tower exposure with high fever, diarrhea, hyponatremia, a lobar pattern, and a positive urine antigen points to Legionella pneumophila.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is acquired from contaminated water aerosols such as hotel cooling towers, and outbreaks cluster among people at one site. Fever above 104 F occurs in about 20% of patients, watery diarrhea in 25-50%, and hyponatremia (sodium below 131) is a recognized clinical clue. Unlike the other atypicals, Legionnaires' disease commonly shows a lobar pattern on imaging, and the urine antigen test is the rapid confirmatory test described for this organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes mild atypical pneumonia with diffuse patchy opacities and is diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification, not urine antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds and is not transmitted by contaminated water systems.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. pneumoniae causes gradual, mild walking pneumonia with interstitial infiltrates and is not detected by a urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia but is not linked to cooling-tower outbreaks, diarrhea, or hyponatremia in this brick.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has had a dry, hacking cough, low-grade fever, malaise, and headache for 3 weeks. Several students on his dormitory floor have had similar illnesses. He looks well and walks into clinic unassisted, but chest radiograph shows streaky, patchy interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than his symptoms suggest. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Mild, gradual-onset 'walking pneumonia' in a young adult with dormitory clustering and radiographic findings out of proportion to symptoms is classic for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired and atypical pneumonia in children and young adults, and outbreaks occur in college dorms, military barracks, and daycares. It is often called walking pneumonia because the illness is mild and self-limiting. Lung involvement frequently appears more severe than the patient's symptoms suggest, with streaky or patchy interstitial infiltrates on imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. psittaci requires contact with infected birds, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Legionnaires' disease typically affects patients over 40 and presents with high fever and a lobar pattern, not a mild 3-week course in a well-appearing student.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is listed as a cause of severe pneumonia in ICU patients, not mild ambulatory illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae causes rapid-onset illness with a productive cough and lobar consolidation.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pet-store employee who recently began caring for newly arrived macaws and cockatoos develops 10 days of fever, fatigue, sore throat, and a dry cough. Chest radiograph shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Atypical pneumonia in a person with occupational bird exposure is psittacosis, caused by Chlamydia psittaci.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. psittaci is named for its association with psittacine birds such as parrots, cockatoos, and macaws. It is not transmitted person to person; infection follows contact with infected birds, so cases occur in people who work around birds or keep them as pets. Its clinical picture is otherwise indistinguishable from C. pneumoniae, ranging from flu-like illness to severe pneumonia with high fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae presents identically but spreads person to person by respiratory droplets, with no bird link.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H. influenzae is a typical pathogen causing productive cough and is not bird associated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L. pneumophila comes from contaminated water aerosols and usually causes higher fever with a lobar pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. pneumoniae spreads person to person and has no zoonotic reservoir described here.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought in with fever and a rash that began on his face and spread to his trunk. Over the past day he has developed painful erosions of the lips and oral mucosa, and examination shows target-like lesions with skin detachment over about 10% of the body surface. He had a respiratory illness with a dry cough 2 weeks ago and takes no medications. Which of the following organisms most likely triggered his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most frequently identified infectious trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially in children and adolescents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and its more severe form, toxic epidermal necrolysis, involve painful rashes and blisters of skin and mucous membranes at sites such as the lips, nose, eyes, and genitals. The mechanism is an immune-mediated response triggered by certain infections and medications that causes cell death and detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes. Although medications are the most common cause overall, among infections M. pneumoniae is the one most often identified, particularly in this age group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia but is not identified as a common trigger of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci can disseminate to liver, heart, and brain, but is not the typical trigger of this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila causes severe pneumonia with gastrointestinal symptoms, not this mucocutaneous syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a typical pneumonia pathogen and is not linked to this syndrome here.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with 2 weeks of gradual-onset malaise and a dry cough is treated with high-dose amoxicillin for presumed pneumonia. She shows no improvement after several days, and sputum culture on routine media grows nothing. Which of the following features of the responsible organism best explains the failure of therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alternates between elementary and reticulate bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion inside macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has no cell wall for the drug to act on

choices.label: D
choices.text: It hides within a large cytoplasmic inclusion body

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes an enzyme that destroys the drug

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall, so antibiotics that inhibit cell wall synthesis are inherently ineffective.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is the tiniest free-living organism capable of self-replication and lacks a cell wall entirely, which also makes it pleomorphic. Because beta-lactams work by inhibiting cell wall synthesis, they have no target in this organism. Atypical pneumonia is in fact defined as pneumonia caused by non-classical pathogens that do not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The elementary and reticulate body cycle belongs to Chlamydia species, not Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion is how Legionella survives in macrophages and does not explain beta-lactam failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth inside a large inclusion body is a Chlamydia feature, not a Mycoplasma feature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-lactamase production is not described as the mechanism of resistance for this organism.

questions.stem: A respiratory isolate from a young adult with atypical pneumonia will grow only on media supplemented with cholesterol, and after prolonged incubation the colonies have a characteristic fried-egg appearance. Which of the following organisms is most consistent with these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia pneumoniae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae requires sterols in its culture medium and forms fried-egg colonies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sterols are present in the M. pneumoniae cell membrane, a feature rare among bacteria, and culturing the organism therefore requires that sterols be present in the media. In culture the colonies take on a fried-egg appearance, and the memory hook offered is that eggs contain cholesterol, linking the colony shape to the growth requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. pneumoniae is an obligate intracellular organism that requires cell culture rather than enriched agar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. psittaci likewise grows only inside living host cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L. pneumophila needs iron and cysteine on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, not sterols.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae grows readily on standard laboratory media without added sterols.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 35-year-old is diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia and will be treated as an outpatient. Besides Streptococcus pneumoniae and respiratory viruses, which of the following groups of organisms are among the most common causes of pneumonia in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Legionella species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacilli, Staphylococcus aureus, and Chlamydia psittaci

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legionella species, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella species, and gram-negative bacilli

explanation.summary: Outpatient community-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and respiratory viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microbial causes of community-acquired pneumonia differ by site of care. In outpatients, the listed organisms are S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, C. pneumoniae, and respiratory viruses. Legionella species appear among hospitalized non-ICU and ICU patients, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli appear in the ICU group, reflecting more severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C. trachomatis causes urethritis and eye infections rather than community-acquired pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative bacilli and S. aureus are ICU-associated, and C. psittaci requires bird exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella is a hospitalized-patient pathogen here, and C. trachomatis is not a pneumonia pathogen in this list.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are the organisms listed for ICU patients with severe pneumonia, not ambulatory patients.

questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae must first attach to ciliated epithelial cells of the lower airway before it can enter cells and establish infection. Which of the following mediates this attachment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A thick polysaccharide capsule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flagella and pili on the bacterial surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipopolysaccharide O antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surface proteins of the elementary body

choices.label: E
choices.text: The adhesin protein P1

explanation.summary: P1 is the virulence factor by which M. pneumoniae binds ciliated respiratory epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae attaches to respiratory epithelial cells using the virulence factor P1, which binds ciliated epithelial cells in the lungs and facilitates entry of the bacteria into cells. After attachment there is roughly a 2 to 3 week incubation period before the gradual onset of symptoms, which is why the illness is easy to miss early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A capsule is not among the virulence factors described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flagella and pili are how L. pneumophila attaches to respiratory epithelium and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M. pneumoniae has no cell wall and is not described as using an O antigen for adherence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elementary bodies are the infectious form of Chlamydia species, not a Mycoplasma structure.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man shares a dormitory room with a student who has just been diagnosed with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. If he becomes infected, approximately how long after exposure would symptoms be expected to begin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 2 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 to 3 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3 to 6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4 to 6 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 6 to 12 hours

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae has a roughly 2 to 3 week incubation period followed by gradual onset of symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: After P1-mediated attachment to ciliated epithelium, there is approximately a 2 to 3 week incubation period before symptoms begin gradually. This long incubation and insidious onset contrast with the 2 to 10 day incubation and rapid progression seen with Legionnaires' disease, and they help explain why outbreaks in closed settings unfold slowly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to two days is far shorter than the incubation described for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Months-long latency is not described for M. pneumoniae.
