whyWrongByChoice.D: Four to six days approximates the Legionella range, which is 2 to 10 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incubation of hours would suggest a toxin-mediated illness, not Mycoplasma infection.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 10-day history of dry cough, low-grade fever, and headache, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is suspected. Which of the following tests provides the most accurate and rapid confirmation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinin titer on chilled serum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram stain of expectorated sputum

choices.label: D
choices.text: PCR performed on a respiratory specimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine antigen immunoassay

explanation.summary: PCR is the most accurate and rapid way to diagnose Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: None of the clinical manifestations of M. pneumoniae infection are distinct enough to separate it from other atypical pneumonias, and the organism grows only on specialized Eaton agar over weeks. As with viruses, PCR can be performed on patient samples, and it is explicitly the most accurate and rapid way to establish the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold agglutination is nonspecific and is no longer recommended now that better tests exist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar is the medium for Legionella, and Mycoplasma requires sterol-containing media.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism has no cell wall and is not seen on Gram stain of sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urine antigen test described in this brick detects Legionella, not Mycoplasma.

questions.stem: A resident proposes mixing a patient's serum with red blood cells and chilling the mixture to support a presumptive diagnosis of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Which of the following is the best reason this test is no longer recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be performed once antibiotics are started

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects only a single serotype of the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is nonspecific; other conditions cause agglutination

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires living host cells to propagate the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires several weeks of incubation to be read

explanation.summary: Cold agglutination testing has been abandoned because it is not specific and better tests are now available.
explanation.whyCorrect: Historically, cold agglutination tests supported a diagnosis of M. pneumoniae: patient serum was mixed with red blood cells and chilled, and antibodies caused the cells to clump. Combined with the clinical picture it served as a quick presumptive test, but it is not specific because other conditions also cause cold agglutination. Since more specific tests such as PCR are now available, cold agglutination is no longer recommended.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prior antibiotic use is not the stated limitation of this test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Detection of only one serotype describes the Legionella urine antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Requiring living host cells describes Chlamydia culture, not a serum agglutination assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weeks of incubation describes Eaton agar culture, not the agglutination test, which is quick.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old with patchy interstitial infiltrates has sputum and blood cultures that show no growth after 48 hours, and the team concludes the illness must be viral. Which of the following best explains the negative cultures if Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It circulates only in blood and never in the airway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It grows only within living host cells and cannot be cultured

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is destroyed by the transport medium used for sputum

choices.label: D
choices.text: It needs iron and cysteine that standard media lack

choices.label: E
choices.text: It needs specialized Eaton agar and weeks of incubation

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes culture-negative pneumonia because it requires specialized Eaton agar and weeks of growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae can be cultured only on specialized Eaton agar, which is not typically stocked in clinical laboratories, and the culture takes weeks. As a result the organism produces culture-negative pneumonia, which makes a virus appear to be the cause and contributes to the infection being underdiagnosed. Rapid PCR testing is what resolves the picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The organism infects the respiratory tract and is transmitted by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Obligate intracellular growth requiring cell culture describes Chlamydia species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction by transport medium is not the explanation given for negative cultures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron and cysteine requirements belong to the fastidious Legionella pneumophila.

questions.stem: A student observes that Chlamydia species have an outer membrane and are therefore gram-negative by structure, yet organisms are not seen on Gram stain of clinical specimens. Which of the following best explains this discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are acid-fast and need a Ziehl-Neelsen stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are coated by a thick waxy mycolic acid layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain sterols in place of a cell wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: They exist only as free extracellular spores

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack classic peptidoglycan and are very small

explanation.summary: Chlamydia species are gram-negative by structure but do not stain with Gram stain because they lack classic peptidoglycan and are very small.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia species have an outer membrane, which makes them gram-negative structurally, but they lack classic peptidoglycan and do not take up the Gram stain. Their poor gram staining and small size made them difficult to visualize by light microscopy, which is one reason they were originally mistaken for viruses until advances in microscopy and molecular biology proved they were bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlamydia species are not acid-fast organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A waxy mycolic acid layer characterizes acid-fast bacteria, a separate category from the atypicals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sterols in the membrane and absence of a cell wall describe Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elementary bodies are spore-like but the organism also has an intracellular replicating form.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of Chlamydia species best explains why they cannot be grown on cell-free laboratory media?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They divide only inside macrophage phagolysosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: They grow only at temperatures above 40 C

choices.label: C
choices.text: They need sterols supplied in the growth medium

choices.label: D
choices.text: They require added iron and cysteine to divide

choices.label: E
choices.text: They use host cell ATP and grow only inside cells

explanation.summary: Chlamydia species are obligate intracellular bacteria that depend on host cell ATP, so a cell culture is required to grow them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia species lack classic peptidoglycan, rely on host cell ATP, and are obligate intracellular bacteria. Because of this dependence, growing them requires a cell culture rather than ordinary agar, which is both costly and time consuming. That limitation is a major reason nucleic acid amplification testing has replaced culture for laboratory identification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlamydia replicates in an endosomal inclusion whose fusion with lysosomes it actively prevents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No unusual temperature requirement is described for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sterol-supplemented media are needed for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron and cysteine requirements describe the fastidious Legionella pneumophila.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the form of Chlamydia that is infectious, spore-like, and able to survive outside of host cells to initiate a new infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coiled phagosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elementary body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fried-egg colony

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inclusion body

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulate body

explanation.summary: The elementary body is the infectious, environmentally stable form of Chlamydia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Chlamydia life cycle has two predominant forms. Elementary bodies are infectious, spore-like particles that survive outside host cells and initiate infection, while reticulate bodies are non-infectious, metabolically active forms that replicate within host cells. The cycle begins when elementary bodies attach to a target cell determined by tropism and are taken up by endocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coiling phagocytosis describes the uptake of Legionella by macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fried-egg colonies describe the appearance of Mycoplasma pneumoniae in culture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inclusion body is the enlarged endosome in which the organism replicates, not a bacterial form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reticulate body is non-infectious and exists only inside host cells.

questions.stem: After a Chlamydia particle is taken up by endocytosis, it converts into a metabolically active form that multiplies within the endosome. Which of the following correctly names this form and its mode of replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elementary body, binary fission in the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elementary body, budding from the host membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reticulate body, binary fission inside the inclusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulate body, fusion with host lysosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulate body, sporulation within the nucleus

explanation.summary: Inside the endosome, elementary bodies convert to reticulate bodies that replicate by binary fission within the enlarging inclusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once inside the endosome, Chlamydia changes from elementary bodies to reticulate bodies. The reticulate bodies replicate by binary fission within the inclusionary body, using host machinery, and the inclusion enlarges as they multiply. After several rounds of division some reticulate bodies differentiate back into elementary bodies, and the infected cell eventually lyses to release them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The replicating form is the reticulate body, and it divides inside the inclusion rather than free in cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elementary bodies do not replicate, and budding is not the described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The organism prevents rather than promotes lysosomal fusion with the endosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chlamydia does not sporulate or replicate inside the host nucleus.

questions.stem: Chlamydia species survive and multiply after being taken into an epithelial cell by endocytosis. Which of the following best accounts for this intracellular survival?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They coat themselves in host antibody to avoid detection

choices.label: B
choices.text: They escape into the cytoplasm using a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit the enzymes of the host oxidative burst

choices.label: D
choices.text: They neutralize the phagolysosome by producing ammonia

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prevent lysosomes from fusing with the endosome

explanation.summary: Chlamydia species are experts at preventing lysosome fusion with the endosome, allowing them to replicate in a protected inclusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: After endocytosis the organism resides in an endosome referred to as an inclusionary body. Chlamydia species prevent fusion of lysosomes with this endosome, so once inside cells they make the endosome their home and divide rapidly. The inclusion can become so large that it occupies the majority of the cell volume before the cell lyses and releases new elementary bodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody coating is not described as a survival strategy for these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chlamydia remains within the inclusion rather than escaping into the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting oxidative burst enzymes is not the mechanism attributed to Chlamydia in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ammonia-mediated neutralization of the phagolysosome is not the mechanism described here.

questions.stem: A laboratory wishes to visualize chlamydial inclusions directly in cells from a clinical specimen. Which of the following stains is most appropriate for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gram stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: India ink preparation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iodine stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silver stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain

explanation.summary: Chlamydial inclusion bodies can be demonstrated with iodine, Giemsa, or immunofluorescent stains.
explanation.whyCorrect: Visualizing Chlamydia species is extremely difficult because of their small size and unique life cycle, but the inclusion bodies they form inside host cells can be stained with iodine, Giemsa, or immunofluorescent stains. Iodine staining of inclusions is one of the classic microscopic approaches, though nucleic acid amplification has largely replaced staining for routine identification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlamydia species do not take up the Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: India ink is used for encapsulated organisms and is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silver stain is used for Legionella pneumophila in sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ziehl-Neelsen is an acid-fast stain and is not used for these organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common method used by clinical laboratories to identify Chlamydia species today?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell culture of the clinical specimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cold agglutinin titer on chilled serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine antigen immunoassay

explanation.summary: Nucleic acid amplification testing (PCR) is the most common laboratory method for identifying Chlamydia species.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because Chlamydia species are obligate intracellular organisms, culture requires a cell culture system that is costly and time consuming, and staining methods were time consuming and inconsistent. For these reasons nucleic acid amplification testing is now the most common way to identify Chlamydia in the laboratory, and most labs have automated systems that process many samples within hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cell culture is possible but too costly and slow for routine identification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cold agglutinins were historically associated with Mycoplasma and are nonspecific.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar is the medium for Legionella pneumophila.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urine antigen test described here is specific to Legionella pneumophila.

questions.stem: Two patients have atypical pneumonia that is clinically indistinguishable; one is infected with Chlamydia pneumoniae and the other with Chlamydia psittaci. Which of the following best distinguishes these two organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C. psittaci forms inclusion bodies and C. pneumoniae does not

choices.label: B
choices.text: C. psittaci is acquired from birds, not from other people

choices.label: C
choices.text: C. psittaci is identified by a rapid urine antigen test

choices.label: D
choices.text: C. psittaci lacks a cell wall while C. pneumoniae has one

choices.label: E
choices.text: C. psittaci produces lobar rather than interstitial infiltrates

explanation.summary: C. pneumoniae and C. psittaci cause indistinguishable respiratory illness; the difference is the route of acquisition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinically, C. pneumoniae and C. psittaci are very similar and both cause respiratory tract infections that cannot be told apart on presentation. The big difference is that C. psittaci is not transmitted person to person; it is contracted by contact with infected birds and is named for its association with psittacine birds such as parrots, cockatoos, and macaws. C. pneumoniae spreads by respiratory droplets and person-to-person contact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both organisms are obligate intracellular bacteria that form inclusion bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urine antigen testing is used for Legionella, not for either Chlamydia species.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither organism is distinguished by absence of a cell wall; that describes Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both produce interstitial and patchy opacities; a lobar pattern suggests Legionella.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old bird breeder hospitalized with severe pneumonia develops jaundice with elevated transaminases, chest pain with new arrhythmias, and confusion. Which of the following best characterizes these new findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia caused by cold agglutinins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pontiac fever complicating the pneumonia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reactive airway disease caused by the infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome triggered by the infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic spread causing hepatitis and encephalitis

explanation.summary: Psittacosis is usually self-limiting, but rare systemic complications include hepatitis, myocarditis, and encephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The typical presentation of C. psittaci ranges from moderate flu-like symptoms to severe pneumonia with high fever. Rarely, systemic complications occur, including hepatitis, myocarditis, and encephalitis, which match this patient's liver, cardiac, and neurologic findings. Most cases are self-limiting, and immunocompromise is associated with severe or disseminated disease; psittacosis can rarely be lethal, as in a 2024 European outbreak that killed five people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold agglutinins relate to an outdated Mycoplasma test and do not explain these organ findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pontiac fever is a mild self-limiting flu-like illness caused by Legionella without pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive airway disease is an upper respiratory manifestation of Mycoplasma infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome involves skin and mucous membrane blistering, not hepatitis and myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia acquired after a stay at a resort has a negative Legionella urine antigen test, yet the clinical picture still strongly suggests Legionnaires' disease and PCR is subsequently positive. Which of the following best explains the negative antigen result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The test cannot be used in immunocompromised patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: The test cross-reacts only with chlamydial antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: The test detects only serotype 1 of the organism

choices.label: D
choices.text: The test requires that the patient produce sputum

choices.label: E
choices.text: The test turns positive only after 2 weeks of illness

explanation.summary: The common Legionella urine test detects only serotype 1, so infection with another serotype gives a negative result.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila antigens can be detected in blood and urine with a rapid immunoassay, but the most common urine test detects only serotype 1. That serotype causes about 90% of all cases of Legionnaires' disease, which is why the test is so useful in the field, but the remaining serotypes will be missed. For that reason PCR and/or culture and staining are performed to cover the additional serotypes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunocompromise does not preclude antigen testing in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The test targets Legionella antigen and is not described as cross-reacting with Chlamydia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The test is done on urine, which is an advantage when patients produce no sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A two-week delay to positivity is not a described limitation of the antigen test.

questions.stem: A laboratory is attempting to culture Legionella pneumophila from a respiratory specimen. Which of the following growth requirements must be met?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chocolate agar supplying X and V factors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron and cysteine in charcoal yeast extract agar

choices.label: C
choices.text: Living eukaryotic cells in a tissue culture system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sterols must be added to the culture medium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strictly anaerobic incubation with added carbon dioxide

explanation.summary: Legionella pneumophila is fastidious and grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, which supplies iron and cysteine.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is a fastidious organism that requires iron and cysteine, and it is grown on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, sometimes simply called charcoal agar. Culture is used along with PCR because the common urine antigen test misses serotypes other than serotype 1. The agar used to grow this organism is noted to be a frequently tested point.

whyWrongByChoice.A: X and V factors on chocolate agar support Haemophilus influenzae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tissue culture with living cells is required for the obligate intracellular Chlamydia species.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sterol-containing media are required for Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anaerobic incubation is not among the described requirements for this organism.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected Legionnaires' disease produces a sputum sample. Gram stain shows numerous neutrophils but no visible organisms. Which of the following stains is most likely to demonstrate the bacteria in this specimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acid-fast stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Giemsa stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: India ink preparation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iodine stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silver stain

explanation.summary: Legionella stains very poorly with Gram stain, so silver stain is used when sputum is available.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is gram-negative by structure but stains very poorly with the Gram stain, which is why numerous neutrophils with no visible organisms on Gram stain of respiratory secretions is itself listed as a clinical clue for Legionnaires' disease. Silver stain can be used if sputum is produced, and the silver stain is noted to be a commonly tested point.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acid-fast staining applies to mycobacteria, a different category of organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giemsa is likewise a stain used for chlamydial inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: India ink is not described as a method for identifying this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iodine staining is used to demonstrate chlamydial inclusion bodies.

questions.stem: Compared with the pneumonias caused by Mycoplasma and Chlamydia species, the chest radiograph in Legionnaires' disease more commonly shows which of the following patterns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A completely normal radiograph

choices.label: B
choices.text: A diffuse miliary pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lobar consolidation pattern

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper lobe cavitary lesions

explanation.summary: Unlike the other atypicals, Legionnaires' disease commonly shows a lobar pneumonia pattern on imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionnaires' disease shares features with other atypical pneumonias, such as a nonproductive cough and fever, but it differs in important ways. Its incubation is short at 2 to 10 days, it can progress as rapidly as a typical pneumonia, and it commonly presents as a lobar pneumonia pattern on imaging rather than the interstitial pattern seen with Mycoplasma or Chlamydia species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Patients with Legionnaires' disease have radiographic abnormalities, often a dense consolidation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A miliary pattern is not associated with Legionella in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hilar lymphadenopathy is not the imaging pattern described for any of these organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cavitation is not a described feature of atypical bacterial pneumonia here.

questions.stem: Legionella pneumophila persists and multiplies inside alveolar macrophages after being taken up. Which of the following best explains this ability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts into a spore-like elementary body

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inserts sterols into the phagosomal membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lyses the macrophage immediately after being ingested

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replicates only within the extracellular mucus layer

explanation.summary: Legionella is a facultative intracellular pathogen that blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion inside macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila attaches to respiratory epithelial cells and macrophages using flagella and pili. Once taken up by macrophages, it prevents fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes, which allows it to persist inside the macrophage and multiply. During this uptake process it induces a distinctive coiling phagocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elementary bodies are the infectious form of Chlamydia species, not of Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sterols in the membrane are a feature of Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immediate lysis would prevent the intracellular replication that defines this organism's strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Legionella is a facultative intracellular pathogen, not a purely extracellular one.

questions.stem: Legionella pneumophila persists for long periods in cooling towers, fountains, and plumbing systems. Replication within which of the following organisms allows it to survive in these aqueous environments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biofilm-forming environmental fungi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciliated respiratory epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating human red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free-living amoebas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Psittacine birds such as parrots

explanation.summary: In addition to humans, L. pneumophila infects amoebas in order to survive in aqueous environments.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila can infect amoebas in order to persist in water systems, which is why cooling towers, evaporative condensers, swamp coolers, humidifiers, fountains, showers, faucets, and whirlpool baths can all serve as sources of infection. Even the misters in grocery store produce aisles have tested positive for the organism. Humans acquire it by aspiration or direct inhalation of contaminated water.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fungi are not described as a host for Legionella survival in water systems.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciliated respiratory epithelium is the human target of Mycoplasma P1 adherence, not an environmental reservoir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella is not described as replicating inside red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Birds are the reservoir for Chlamydia psittaci, not for Legionella.

questions.stem: During an outbreak investigation at a hotel, several previously healthy guests report 3 days of fever, myalgias, and headache without cough or radiographic pneumonia. All recover fully within a week without treatment. Which of the following best describes this illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pontiac fever caused by Legionella pneumophila

choices.label: B
choices.text: Psittacosis from environmental bird contact

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prodrome of Stevens-Johnson syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tracheobronchitis caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Walking pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Pontiac fever is the self-limiting, flu-like form of Legionella infection that resolves in 3 to 6 days without treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila causes two main diseases: Legionnaires' disease, which is a pneumonia, and Pontiac fever. Pontiac fever's symptoms closely resemble the flu and typically resolve in 3 to 6 days with no medical intervention. It is rarely diagnosed and is usually dismissed as the flu except when it is recognized during an outbreak of Legionnaires' disease, exactly as in this scenario.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Psittacosis requires bird contact and usually produces pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents with rash, blisters, and mucosal erosions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydial tracheobronchitis produces a persistent cough rather than a 3-day flu-like illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Walking pneumonia involves a persistent cough and radiographic infiltrates, which are absent here.

questions.stem: The wife of a man hospitalized with Legionnaires' disease asks whether she is likely to catch the infection from him. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It comes from contaminated water, not from people

choices.label: B
choices.text: She can acquire it from his respiratory droplets

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is at risk only if she handles his sputum

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is at risk only if she is immunocompromised

choices.label: E
choices.text: She should receive antibiotic prophylaxis for 10 days

explanation.summary: Legionella cannot be transmitted from person to person; it is acquired from environmental water sources.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is transmitted from the environment to a person, typically originating from a contaminated water source, and it cannot be transmitted person to person. The organism enters the lungs through aspiration or direct inhalation of contaminated water aerosols, which is why outbreaks are traced to cooling towers, showers, fountains, and similar sources rather than to infected contacts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Respiratory droplet spread applies to M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae, not Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sputum contact is not a described route of transmission for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunocompromise raises the risk of severe disease after environmental exposure, not of person-to-person spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prophylaxis of contacts is unnecessary when the organism does not spread between people.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with pneumonia has not improved after 3 days of ceftriaxone. Which of the following additional findings would most support a presumptive diagnosis of Legionnaires' disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rising cold agglutinin titer

choices.label: B
choices.text: A serum sodium concentration of 126 mEq/L

choices.label: C
choices.text: An elevated serum IgE concentration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral blood eosinophilia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sputum culture growing gram-positive diplococci

explanation.summary: Hyponatremia is one of the clinical clues that, taken together with other findings, supports a presumptive diagnosis of Legionnaires' disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical clues suggestive of Legionnaires' disease include diarrhea, high fever above 104 F, numerous neutrophils but no organisms on Gram stain of respiratory secretions, hyponatremia, failure to respond to beta-lactam and aminoglycoside antibiotics, and illness linked to an environment associated with Legionella. A sodium of 126 falls in the hyponatremic range that is characteristic. None of these findings is specific alone, but collectively they support a presumptive diagnosis, and Legionella is the most lethal of the atypical bacterial pneumonias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold agglutinins were historically linked to Mycoplasma and are nonspecific.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated IgE is not a described feature of Legionnaires' disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eosinophilia is not listed among the clinical clues for this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gram-positive diplococci indicate Streptococcus pneumoniae, a typical pathogen that responds to beta-lactams.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia develops a widespread skin eruption, and blood cultures and biopsies suggest spread beyond the lungs. Which of the following best characterizes disseminated Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is prevented by early beta-lactam therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is rare and most commonly causes skin rashes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is seen mainly in healthy young athletes

choices.label: D
choices.text: It most commonly manifests as acute renal failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: It occurs in the majority of infected patients

explanation.summary: Disseminated M. pneumoniae infection is rare, tied to severe immunocompromise, and most often manifests as skin rashes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dissemination is an uncommon complication of M. pneumoniae pneumonia and is associated with severe immunocompromise, such as advanced HIV infection. When it does occur, the most common manifestation, in roughly 20% of cases, is skin rashes. Most patients, by contrast, have a mild self-limiting illness or no symptoms at all.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-lactams are ineffective against an organism that has no cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dissemination is associated with severe immunocompromise, not with healthy hosts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal failure is not the described manifestation of disseminated infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only a few people who acquire the organism even develop pneumonia, let alone disseminated disease.

questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae accounts for approximately what proportion of all cases of community-acquired pneumonia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Less than 1 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: 10 to 25 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: 30 to 45 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: 50 to 60 percent

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes roughly 10 to 25 percent of community-acquired pneumonia cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, accounting for roughly 10 to 25% of all cases, and it is also the leading cause of atypical pneumonia. It can affect any demographic, but outbreaks frequently occur in college dorms, military barracks, and daycares, and by adulthood most people have circulating antibodies indicating prior infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few percent corresponds to the Legionella share of community-acquired pneumonia, which is about 2 to 9%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Less than 1% would make the organism rare, which contradicts its status as a leading cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the contribution of this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No single atypical organism accounts for half of community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.stem: Infection with Chlamydia pneumoniae characteristically begins with upper respiratory tract symptoms before progressing to bronchitis or pneumonia. Which of the following sets of symptoms is most typical of this early phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjunctivitis and genital discharge

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jaundice, arrhythmias, and confusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharyngitis, sinusitis, and otitis media

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target lesions and painful mucosal erosions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Watery diarrhea and abdominal pain

explanation.summary: C. pneumoniae typically starts with upper respiratory symptoms such as pharyngitis, rhinitis, sinusitis, and otitis media.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. pneumoniae commonly presents with upper respiratory tract symptoms first that then progress to bronchitis and/or pneumonia. The common upper respiratory symptoms are pharyngitis, rhinitis, sinusitis, and otitis media. Respiratory symptoms then parallel M. pneumoniae with a persistent dry cough, moderate fever, headache, and fatigue, usually lasting 1 to 2 weeks with cough persisting for several weeks afterward.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjunctival and genital involvement reflects C. trachomatis tropism, not C. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These organ findings represent rare systemic complications of psittacosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target lesions and mucosal erosions describe Stevens-Johnson syndrome, linked to M. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diarrhea and abdominal pain are gastrointestinal features of Legionnaires' disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following clinical patterns best distinguishes an atypical pneumonia from a typical bacterial pneumonia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abrupt onset with rigors and blood-streaked sputum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete absence of fever, malaise, and headache

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gradual onset with mild symptoms and a dry cough

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleuritic chest pain with lobar consolidation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid onset of illness with a productive cough

explanation.summary: Atypical pneumonias tend to present with mild symptoms, a dry nonproductive cough, and gradual onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atypical pneumonia is defined as pneumonia caused by non-classical pathogens that do not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics, and it often presents with mild symptoms, a dry nonproductive cough, and gradual onset. Pneumonias caused by typical organisms commonly present with rapid onset of symptoms and a productive cough. This is a rule of thumb rather than an absolute, since dehydrated patients or those with poor lung function may not produce sputum even with a typical bacterium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abrupt onset with rigors points toward a typical organism rather than an atypical one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fever, malaise, and headache are shared by both typical and atypical pneumonias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lobar consolidation pattern is more characteristic of typical pathogens and of Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rapid onset with a productive cough is the pattern of typical bacterial pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old and a 70-year-old are both exposed to aerosolized water from the same contaminated cooling system. The younger patient develops a brief flu-like illness that resolves without treatment, while the older patient develops severe pneumonia requiring admission. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legionnaires' disease mainly strikes patients over 40

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only older adults excrete detectable urinary antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Younger patients acquire the organism only person to person

choices.label: D
choices.text: Younger patients are exposed to a different bacterial serotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: Younger patients clear the organism using cold agglutinins

explanation.summary: Legionnaires' disease targets older and immunocompromised hosts, while younger healthy people exposed to the same source often get only Pontiac fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: L. pneumophila is a major cause of community-acquired pneumonia that typically affects the elderly or the immunocompromised, and patients who develop Legionnaires' disease are usually over 40 years old. Younger, healthy adults exposed to the same contaminated water often develop instead the self-limiting flu-like illness known as Pontiac fever, which resolves in 3 to 6 days without intervention.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Urine antigen detection depends on the infecting serotype, not on patient age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella is never transmitted person to person; both acquired it from the environment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both patients were exposed to the same water source, and serotype does not explain the age difference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cold agglutinins relate to an outdated Mycoplasma test and do not clear Legionella.

questions.stem: Chlamydia species cause genital, respiratory, and ocular disease depending on the species and serotype involved. This pattern reflects tropism for which of the following host cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciliated bronchial epithelium only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Columnar epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free-living environmental amoebas

explanation.summary: Chlamydia species show tropism for columnar epithelial cells of the genital tract, respiratory tract, or conjunctiva.
explanation.whyCorrect: Members of the Chlamydia genus have a tropism for columnar epithelial cells of the genital tract, respiratory tract, or conjunctiva, depending on the species. This explains why C. pneumoniae and C. psittaci are common causes of atypical pneumonia while C. trachomatis is a common cause of bacterial urethritis and eye infections, depending on the serotype. The life cycle begins when elementary bodies attach to whichever target cell the species prefers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveolar macrophages are the intracellular niche of Legionella pneumophila.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Restricting tropism to bronchial epithelium cannot explain genital and ocular infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are not the target cells for chlamydial replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amoebas serve as an environmental host for Legionella, not for Chlamydia.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who hikes weekly in wooded areas of the northeastern United States develops a slowly expanding red rash on his thigh 10 days after a camping trip. He is diagnosed with Lyme disease. The bite of which of the following arthropods most likely transmitted this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amblyomma americanum, the lone star tick

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dermacentor andersoni, the Rocky Mountain wood tick

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dermacentor variabilis, the American dog tick

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged or deer tick

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick

explanation.summary: Lyme disease is transmitted by the bite of the blacklegged (deer) tick, Ixodes scapularis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in mice and is transmitted to humans by Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged or deer tick. Lyme disease occurs most frequently in the northeastern United States, matching this patient's exposure. Ixodes scapularis is also a vector for Ehrlichia species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lone star tick transmits Ehrlichia species and is associated with alpha-gal syndrome, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Rocky Mountain wood tick is one of the ticks that carries Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The American dog tick is a Rocky Mountain spotted fever vector and is the species most often implicated in that disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brown dog tick transmits Rickettsia rickettsii; it is not a vector for Borrelia burgdorferi.

questions.stem: A public health officer is explaining how Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in nature before ticks transmit it to humans. Which of the following serves as the reservoir for this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cattle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Domestic dogs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Humans

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mice

choices.label: E
choices.text: White-tailed deer

explanation.summary: Mice are the reservoir for Borrelia burgdorferi; ticks acquire the organism from them and pass it to humans.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reservoir of Borrelia burgdorferi is mice. Ixodes ticks feed on infected mice and subsequently transmit the spirochete to humans during a prolonged blood meal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cattle are not the reservoir for this spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dogs can be bitten by ticks but are not the reservoir that maintains Borrelia burgdorferi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Humans are incidental, dead-end hosts and do not maintain the organism in nature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deer support the tick life cycle but are not the reservoir named for the spirochete itself.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman finds a tick attached to her calf after gardening and removes it within 2 hours. She asks about her risk of acquiring Lyme disease. Which of the following best explains why her risk is low?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the larval stage of the tick is able to transmit the organism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only ticks that have fed on deer rather than mice carry the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tick must feed for 36 to 48 hours before transmission

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transmission occurs only in autumn, when adult ticks are feeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transmission occurs only when the tick is crushed during removal

explanation.summary: Lyme transmission requires roughly 36 to 48 hours of tick attachment, so prompt removal rarely results in disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: For Lyme disease to occur, the tick must be attached for 36 to 48 hours. Removing the tick promptly after the bite rarely results in disease, which is why tick checks after outdoor exposure are effective prevention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nymph is the stage usually responsible for transmission, and adults can transmit as well.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mice are the reservoir; the risk relationship described here is not what determines transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nymphs typically feed in the spring and summer, when most transmission occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission depends on duration of attachment, not on whether the tick is crushed.

questions.stem: Most patients who acquire Lyme disease never notice the tick that bit them, and most transmission occurs in the spring and summer. Which stage of Ixodes scapularis is usually responsible for transmitting the infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult female

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adult male

choices.label: C
choices.text: Egg

choices.label: D
choices.text: Larva

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nymph

explanation.summary: The immature nymph is the usual culprit in Lyme transmission because it is small enough to go unnoticed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The nymph form of Ixodes scapularis is the usual culprit because nymphs are very small and easily go unnoticed, allowing them to stay attached long enough to transmit the spirochete. Nymphs typically feed in the spring and summer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult females can transmit the organism, but their larger size means they are usually seen and removed first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adult males, like adult females, are large enough to be noticed and removed before transmission occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eggs do not feed on hosts and cannot transmit infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The larva is not identified as the usual transmitting stage for human Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man develops a red, slowly expanding rash with a target-like appearance on his flank 12 days after a tick bite. Which of the following skin findings is pathognomonic for Lyme disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bullous lesions scattered over the trunk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythema migrans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maculopapular rash beginning on the wrists

choices.label: D
choices.text: Petechial rash involving the palms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicular rash confined to one dermatome

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans, the expanding bull's-eye rash, is pathognomonic for Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema migrans is a red, expanding rash that gradually enlarges and can take on a bull's-eye appearance. It is pathognomonic for Lyme disease and, when present, allows a clinical diagnosis before serology becomes positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bullous lesions are not a common presentation of Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A maculopapular rash starting on the wrists and ankles is the pattern seen in Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A petechial rash is more characteristic of Rocky Mountain spotted fever as its vasculitis progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A dermatomal vesicular rash is not among the rashes described for Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A physician counsels a patient that the absence of the characteristic Lyme rash does not exclude the diagnosis. Approximately what proportion of patients with Lyme disease develop erythema migrans?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10 to 20 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: 30 to 40 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: 50 to 60 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: 70 to 80 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: 95 to 100 percent

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans appears in roughly 70 to 80 percent of patients with Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rash is present in about 70 to 80 percent of patients, meaning that a substantial minority never develop it. More than 30 percent of patients never get the classic bull's-eye appearance, and the rash may take many atypical forms or be absent entirely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the frequency of the hallmark rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is closer to the proportion who never develop the classic bull's-eye form, not the proportion with any rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This underestimates the frequency with which erythema migrans appears.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rash is not nearly universal; atypical presentations without rash are well recognized.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops several new annular rashes, shooting pains in his arms and legs, and a right-sided facial droop 6 weeks after a tick bite. An electrocardiogram shows heart block. Which structure is most commonly involved in the conduction abnormality at this stage of Lyme disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrioventricular node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bundle of His

choices.label: C
choices.text: Left bundle branch

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purkinje fiber network

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sinoatrial node

explanation.summary: Heart block in early disseminated Lyme disease usually involves the atrioventricular node.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stage 2, early disseminated Lyme disease, occurs within weeks to months of the bite and features multiple rashes, dispersed musculoskeletal pain, meningitis, facial (Bell) palsy, inflammation of the heart, and heart block that usually involves the atrioventricular node.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Block at the bundle of His is not the characteristic site of involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated left bundle branch block is not the typical conduction finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Purkinje network is not the usual site of Lyme carditis conduction block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sinoatrial node dysfunction is not the conduction abnormality described in disseminated Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has recurrent swollen, warm knee joints beginning 14 months after an untreated tick-borne illness acquired in Connecticut. Which of the following best characterizes the arthritis of late disseminated Lyme disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymmetric, intermittent large-joint involvement, especially the knees

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monoarticular great toe involvement with crystal deposition in fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent axial involvement with fusion of the sacroiliac joints

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symmetric proximal muscle weakness without any joint swelling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symmetric small-joint involvement of the hands with morning stiffness

explanation.summary: Lyme arthritis is asymmetric and intermittent, affects large joints such as the knees, and comes with swelling and warmth.
explanation.whyCorrect: During stage 3, which occurs months to years after the bite, most patients with arthritis have bouts of severe joint inflammation. The arthritis is distinguished from other forms in that it is associated with swelling and warmth, may be migratory, is intermittent, and is often asymmetric, with a predilection for large joints, especially the knees.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Crystal-associated monoarthritis of the great toe describes a different disease process entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Axial disease with sacroiliac fusion is not a feature of late Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late Lyme disease produces joint inflammation with swelling and warmth, not painless proximal muscle weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symmetric small-joint disease of the hands is not the pattern described for Lyme arthritis.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man completed antibiotic therapy for Lyme disease 8 months ago, and there is no evidence of ongoing infection. He still reports muscle and joint pain, cognitive difficulty, disturbed sleep, and fatigue. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coinfection with Rickettsia rickettsii from the same bite

choices.label: B
choices.text: Persistent bacteremia from an inadequate antibiotic dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of latent spirochetes in the nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relapse of Lyme disease from antibiotic-resistant Borrelia burgdorferi

explanation.summary: Lingering symptoms after antibiotics have cleared Borrelia burgdorferi define post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients have lingering symptoms even after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection. Common complaints are muscle and joint pains, cognitive issues, sleep disturbance, and fatigue. The cause is unknown, though there is some evidence for an autoimmune response triggered by Borrelia burgdorferi. It is often colloquially called chronic Lyme disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A rickettsial coinfection would present as an acute febrile illness, not months of fatigue and cognitive complaints.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no ongoing bacteremia; the infection has been documented as cleared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactivation of latent spirochetes is not the described mechanism for persistent post-treatment symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The infection has been cleared; ongoing resistant infection is not the explanation for these symptoms.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of patients treated for Lyme disease continue to have lingering symptoms after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 to 5 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: 10 to 20 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: 30 to 40 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 50 percent

explanation.summary: Roughly 10 to 20 percent of treated patients have persistent symptoms, a condition called post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 10 to 20 percent of patients will have lingering symptoms even after antibiotic therapy has cleared the infection. This is post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, with muscle and joint pains, cognitive issues, sleep disturbance, and fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This markedly underestimates how common persistent post-treatment symptoms are.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is far lower than the reported frequency of persistent symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overestimates the proportion with lingering symptoms after treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Half of treated patients do not go on to have persistent symptoms.

questions.stem: Borrelia burgdorferi is a spirochete. Which of the following structures is responsible for its characteristic motility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polar flagellum anchored outside the outer membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoflagella, also called axial filaments, within the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gliding motility from surface adhesion protein complexes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peritrichous flagella distributed over the cell surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type IV pili that retract to pull the cell forward

explanation.summary: Spirochetes move using endoflagella (axial filaments), a structure internal to the cell envelope.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spirochetes have a complex cell wall resembling that of gram-negative bacteria, with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane, plus a unique structure called an endoflagella or axial filament that contributes to their motility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An externally anchored polar flagellum is not the spirochete arrangement; the flagella lie within the cell envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes do not rely on surface adhesion gliding for movement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritrichous external flagella are found in other bacteria, not in spirochetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type IV pilus-driven twitching motility is not the mechanism used by spirochetes.

questions.stem: A laboratory attempts to visualize Borrelia burgdorferi in a skin biopsy from a patient with suspected Lyme disease. Which of the following best describes this organism's cell wall and staining behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gram-negative envelope that is readily seen on routine Gram stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: A gram-negative-like envelope, but it stains poorly on Gram stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thick peptidoglycan layer that stains crisply as gram-positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: An acid-fast envelope owing to mycolic acids in the cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: No cell wall at all, so that no stain will reveal the organism

explanation.summary: Spirochetes have a gram-negative-type envelope but stain poorly with Gram stain, so special stains are needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi has a complex cell wall similar to that of gram-negative bacteria, with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane. Despite this, spirochetes do not stain well by Gram stain, and special stains must be used for optimal visualization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although the envelope resembles that of gram-negative bacteria, the organism is not readily seen on routine Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The peptidoglycan layer is thin, not thick, and the organism is not gram-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acid-fastness from mycolic acids is a feature of a different group of organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spirochetes do have a cell wall; the problem is that it takes up Gram stain poorly.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for suspected Lyme disease 5 weeks after a tick bite. Which of the following is the recommended laboratory diagnostic pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood culture on chocolate agar incubated for 48 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: ELISA for antibodies, confirmed by a second ELISA or Western blot

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram stain of a punch biopsy taken from the edge of the rash

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect immunofluorescence on two paired serum samples

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine antigen testing for Borrelia cell wall components

explanation.summary: Lyme disease is diagnosed by detecting antibodies with ELISA, confirmed by a second ELISA or Western blot.
explanation.whyCorrect: The recommended diagnostic pathway is detection of antibodies against Borrelia burgdorferi by ELISA, with confirmation by a second ELISA or a Western blot. Western blots can improve sensitivity and can distinguish Borrelia burgdorferi antibodies from antibodies cross-reactive to spirochetes of the microbiota.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Culture is difficult, prolonged, and labor intensive, and is not the recommended diagnostic route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes stain poorly on Gram stain, so this would not reliably identify the organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paired-serum indirect immunofluorescence is the serologic gold standard for Rocky Mountain spotted fever, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine antigen testing is not part of the recommended pathway for Lyme disease.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presents 6 days after a tick bite with an expanding annular rash on his back. Serologic testing for Borrelia burgdorferi is negative. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A negative result means the tick was attached for fewer than 36 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies take weeks to rise, so history and rash guide the diagnosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The negative result excludes Lyme disease with a high degree of certainty

choices.label: D
choices.text: The negative result indicates infection with a different spirochete species

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rash must be unrelated, because serology is definitive this early

explanation.summary: Early in Lyme disease, serology is often negative because antibodies have not yet risen, so history and erythema migrans drive the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibodies against Borrelia burgdorferi are detected in a minority of patients during the early stages of infection and in a much larger share later in disease. Because it takes weeks for antibody levels to rise to detectable levels, patient history of a tick bite and symptoms such as erythema migrans are the most helpful diagnostic tools early in the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serologic results say nothing about how long the tick was attached.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Early serology has limited sensitivity, so a negative result cannot exclude the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A negative early ELISA reflects the timing of the antibody response, not an alternative organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythema migrans is pathognomonic and outweighs an early negative serologic test.

questions.stem: A physician is identifying which patients are at highest risk for severe disease from Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Which of the following groups carries the highest risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults older than 65 years with chronic hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children under 10 years old and those with G6PD deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients with a documented history of prior Lyme disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with sickle cell trait and chronic iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pregnant women in the third trimester of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Children under 10, the immunocompromised, and patients with G6PD deficiency have the highest risk of severe Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: While death from Rocky Mountain spotted fever is rare, it remains the most common cause of death from a tickborne illness in the United States. Children under 10 years of age, immunocompromised patients, and those with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency are at the highest risk for severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Advanced age with hypertension is not among the named high-risk groups.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A history of Lyme disease does not confer risk for severe Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sickle cell trait and iron deficiency are not the enzymatic or immune risk factors described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pregnancy is not identified as a high-risk factor for severe rickettsial disease here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man from North Carolina is diagnosed with Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Which tick species is most commonly implicated in transmission in the states where this disease is most concentrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amblyomma americanum, the lone star tick

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dermacentor andersoni, the Rocky Mountain wood tick

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dermacentor variabilis, the American dog tick

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged tick

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhipicephalus sanguineus, the brown dog tick

explanation.summary: The American dog tick, Dermacentor variabilis, is the species most often implicated in Rocky Mountain spotted fever in the highest-incidence states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several tick species can carry and transmit Rickettsia rickettsii, including Dermacentor variabilis, Dermacentor andersoni, and Rhipicephalus sanguineus. Five states account for half of Rocky Mountain spotted fever cases, and the American dog tick is the species most commonly implicated in transmission in those states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lone star tick is associated with ehrlichiosis and alpha-gal syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Rocky Mountain wood tick can carry the organism, but it is not the species most often implicated in the highest-incidence states.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The blacklegged tick transmits Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis, not Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brown dog tick can carry the organism, but it is not the most commonly implicated species in those states.

questions.stem: Five states account for approximately half of all Rocky Mountain spotted fever cases in the United States. Which of the following lists those states?

choices.label: A
choices.text: California, Oregon, Washington, Nevada, and Idaho

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Connecticut, and Rhode Island

choices.label: C
choices.text: Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, and South Dakota

choices.label: D
choices.text: North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Missouri

choices.label: E
choices.text: Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Louisiana, and Mississippi

explanation.summary: North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Missouri account for about 50 percent of Rocky Mountain spotted fever cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Despite its name, Rocky Mountain spotted fever is most common in central and southern states. North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, and Missouri together account for roughly 50 percent of cases, though cases have been reported as far west as California.

whyWrongByChoice.A: West coast states report cases, but they are not the five highest-burden states.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These northeastern states are the high-incidence region for Lyme disease, not Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mountain west states are not where the disease is most concentrated, despite the name.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These southwestern and gulf states are not the five that account for half of cases.

questions.stem: A microbiology laboratory is unable to grow the organism responsible for a suspected case of Rocky Mountain spotted fever on any routine agar. Which of the following best describes Rickettsia rickettsii?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gram-negative coccobacillus that is an obligate intracellular pathogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A gram-negative diplococcus that grows well on chocolate agar

choices.label: C
choices.text: A gram-positive bacillus that forms spores on routine solid agar

choices.label: D
choices.text: A gram-positive coccus in clusters that grows readily on blood agar

choices.label: E
choices.text: A motile spirochete that can be grown in a specialized liquid broth

explanation.summary: Rickettsia rickettsii is a small, gram-negative, obligate intracellular coccobacillus that cannot be cultured on agar.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rickettsia rickettsii is a small, gram-negative, obligate intracellular coccobacillus. Because it must replicate inside host cells, it cannot be cultured in agar, which is why culture plays no role in diagnosing Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative diplococci describe organisms such as Neisseria, not Rickettsia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rickettsia rickettsii is not a spore-forming gram-positive bacillus and does not grow on agar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram-positive cocci in clusters describe staphylococci, which are unrelated to this illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A motile spirochete describes Borrelia burgdorferi, the agent of Lyme disease.

questions.stem: Two outer membrane proteins of Rickettsia rickettsii both facilitate uptake of the pathogen into host cells and are useful for identifying species within the genus. Which of the following are these proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipooligosaccharide phase variants 1 and 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Outer membrane porin proteins F and D

choices.label: C
choices.text: Outer membrane proteins A and B (OmpA and OmpB)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outer surface proteins A and C (OspA and OspC)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surface M protein and cell wall protein A

explanation.summary: OmpA and OmpB facilitate host cell uptake and are used for species identification within the Rickettsia genus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two outer membrane proteins, outer membrane protein A and outer membrane protein B, are useful for species identification within the Rickettsia genus. The Omp proteins also facilitate uptake of the pathogen by host cells, which is essential for an obligate intracellular organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipooligosaccharide phase variation is not the identification scheme used for this genus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Porin proteins F and D are not the rickettsial proteins used for species identification or uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Outer surface proteins are associated with Borrelia, not with Rickettsia species identification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M protein and protein A are surface proteins of gram-positive cocci, not of Rickettsia.

questions.stem: On average, how long must a tick remain attached to a person before Rickettsia rickettsii is transmitted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1 hour

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 to 5 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 to 10 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: 36 to 48 hours

explanation.summary: Rickettsia rickettsii requires about 6 to 10 hours of tick attachment, far shorter than the 36 to 48 hours needed for Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ticks carry Rickettsia rickettsii after feeding on the blood of infected animals, and the pathogen is transmitted to humans by bite. On average, the tick must be attached to a person for 6 to 10 hours before transmission can occur, a much shorter interval than that required for Borrelia burgdorferi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transmission is not essentially immediate; several hours of attachment are needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Several days of attachment are not required for rickettsial transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the required attachment time for this organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the attachment interval associated with Lyme disease transmission.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with Rocky Mountain spotted fever develops a petechial rash, hypotension, and evidence of diffuse organ dysfunction. Infection of which cell type best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial cells, producing systemic vasculitis throughout the body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocytes, producing massive intravascular hemolysis and anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatocytes, producing fulminant necrosis of the hepatic lobule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mononuclear phagocytes, producing widespread granuloma formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal tubular cells, producing direct nephrotoxic tubular injury

explanation.summary: Rickettsia rickettsii has a strong tropism for endothelial cells, and infecting them causes systemic vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once infected, Rickettsia rickettsii spreads quickly throughout the lymphatic and circulatory systems. The Omp proteins facilitate uptake by cells, and the organism has a strong tropism for endothelial cells. Infection of endothelial cells leads to systemic vasculitis, which explains the petechial rash, the clotting abnormalities, and the multiorgan involvement of severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Rickettsia rickettsii does not parasitize erythrocytes to cause hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocyte infection is not the mechanism underlying rickettsial vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mononuclear phagocytes are the target of Ehrlichia species, not of Rickettsia rickettsii.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal injury in severe disease follows systemic vascular damage rather than direct tubular infection.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman from Arkansas has had fever, severe headache, myalgia, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days after a tick bite. She has no rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate consideration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only about 20 percent of patients ever develop a rash with this illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rash always precedes fever, so this must be an unrelated illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: The absence of a rash on day 3 effectively rules out this diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rash begins on the trunk and then spreads out to the extremities

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rash usually appears 2 to 4 days after the fever has begun

explanation.summary: In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the rash typically lags the fever by 2 to 4 days, so its absence early does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: While about 90 percent of people with Rocky Mountain spotted fever eventually get a rash, it commonly occurs 2 to 4 days after the fever and other initial symptoms present. Fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia are the most common symptoms during the first 3 days, so the diagnosis should be considered even when a rash is absent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Roughly 90 percent of patients eventually develop a rash, not 20 percent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The rash typically follows rather than precedes the fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An absent rash early in the illness is expected and does not exclude the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rash starts peripherally on the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles and spreads toward the trunk.

questions.stem: In early July, a 37-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. Two days ago a maculopapular rash began on her wrists and ankles and has spread to her palms, soles, and trunk; it now shows petechiae. She was bitten by a tick while hiking in a wooded area in Arkansas 2 weeks ago. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Borrelia burgdorferi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ehrlichia chaffeensis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ehrlichia ewingii

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rickettsia rickettsii

explanation.summary: A peripherally starting maculopapular rash with petechiae after an Arkansas tick bite points to Rickettsia rickettsii.
explanation.whyCorrect: The history of tick bite, the location in Arkansas, and the nature of the rash, which starts around the wrists and ankles and spreads to the palms, soles, and trunk, support a presumptive diagnosis of Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Progression to petechiae reflects the systemic vasculitis caused by endothelial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rash of Lyme disease is erythema migrans, a single expanding lesion, not a peripheral maculopapular eruption with petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ehrlichia chaffeensis causes a nonspecific febrile illness without this characteristic peripherally starting rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ehrlichia ewingii causes ehrlichiosis, which does not produce this rash distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis causes ehrlichiosis and does not explain this rash pattern.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with untreated Rocky Mountain spotted fever becomes progressively ill over the course of a week as the organism disseminates through his vascular system. Which of the following complications is characteristic of severe disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia from complete loss of bone marrow precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ascending flaccid paralysis with an entirely normal mental status

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic asymmetric arthritis of large joints such as the knees

choices.label: D
choices.text: Permanent unilateral facial nerve palsy following defervescence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skin and soft tissue necrosis requiring amputation or skin grafts

explanation.summary: Severe Rocky Mountain spotted fever causes vasculitis and clotting that can produce tissue necrosis requiring amputation or grafting.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the pathogen spreads throughout the vascular system, systemic vasculitis and clotting can lead to altered mental status, coma, cerebral edema, respiratory compromise including pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress syndrome, skin and soft tissue necrosis that may result in amputations or skin grafts, and multiorgan damage involving the central nervous system and kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow aplasia is not among the described complications of severe Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Severe disease produces altered mental status and coma rather than an isolated ascending paralysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic large-joint arthritis is a feature of late disseminated Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Facial palsy is characteristic of early disseminated Lyme disease, not of severe rickettsial disease.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the rash is obtained from a patient with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever because the organism stains poorly on Gram stain. Which of the following stains is useful for visualizing Rickettsia rickettsii in tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Giemsa stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: India ink preparation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Periodic acid-Schiff stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ziehl-Neelsen stain

explanation.summary: Rickettsia rickettsii does not stain well with Gram stain but does stain with Giemsa.
explanation.whyCorrect: While Rickettsia rickettsii does not stain well with Gram stain, it does stain with Giemsa, among others. Tissue biopsies of the rash, if present, can therefore be stained and used to identify the pathogen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The organism stains poorly with Gram stain, which is precisely why an alternative stain is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: India ink is used to visualize capsules of certain organisms and has no role here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Periodic acid-Schiff is not the stain used to demonstrate Rickettsia in tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acid-fast staining is used for mycobacteria and is not useful for this organism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the gold standard serologic test for the diagnosis of Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single IgM enzyme immunoassay drawn at presentation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood culture on agar held for 6 to 8 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram stain and culture of a punch biopsy of the rash

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect immunofluorescence on two paired serum samples

choices.label: E
